title: Rights and Citizenship
shortDescription: Types of rights, human rights, statutory rights and constitutional provisions on citizenship (Articles 5–11) and the Citizenship Act, 1955.
genZNote: A right is a claim that society recognises; citizenship is the membership card that unlocks some of them.

sections.heading: Rights — Types and Sources
bullets: Natural/moral rights vs legal and constitutional rights; civil, political, economic, social and cultural rights.
UDHR adopted 10 December 1948; India's statutory body: National Human Rights Commission (Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993).
Constitutional right (not fundamental): property under Art. 300A after the 44th Amendment (1978).
Statutory rights: Right to Information Act, 2005; right to education is a fundamental right under Art. 21A (86th Amendment, 2002).
Some rights (Arts. 15, 16, 19, 29, 30) are available only to citizens; others (Arts. 14, 20–22, 25) to all persons.

sections.heading: Citizenship — Constitution and Act
sections.body: The Citizenship Act, 1955 provides five modes of acquisition: birth, descent, registration, naturalisation and incorporation of territory; loss by renunciation, termination (voluntary foreign acquisition) and deprivation. Naturalisation generally needs 12 years of residence (the Citizenship (Amendment) Act, 2019 reduced it to 5 years for certain persecuted minorities from Afghanistan, Bangladesh and Pakistan who entered before 31 December 2014). India has single citizenship and does not permit dual citizenship; Overseas Citizen of India (OCI) status is not citizenship.

rows: Citizens at commencement of the Constitution

sections.heading: Citizenship by Birth — Timeline
bullets: Born in India between 26 Jan 1950 and 1 July 1987: citizen by birth.
Between 1 July 1987 and 3 Dec 2004: at least one parent a citizen.
After 3 Dec 2004: both parents citizens, or one parent citizen and the other not an illegal migrant.
Figures and rules change — verify against the current text before an exam.

quickRevision.oneLineDefinition: Rights are legally recognised claims; Indian citizenship is governed by Articles 5–11 and the Citizenship Act, 1955.

highYieldFacts: Art. 300A: property is a constitutional right.
commonTraps: Do not say India allows dual citizenship.
